mcqs.question: You are on `main` and run `git merge feature`. `main` has not moved since `feature` branched off it, and `feature` is now two commits ahead. What does Git do by default?
options: Git creates a merge commit anyway, because merging always records where the two branches joined.
Git fast-forwards: `main` moves to `feature`'s tip and no merge commit is created.
Git replays `feature`'s two commits as new commits on `main`, so both of them get new hashes.
Git squashes the two commits into a single commit on `main`, like a host's "Squash and merge" button.
mcqs.explanation: A merge is a pure pointer move whenever the branch being merged is a descendant of the current tip: `--ff` is the default, and its documented behaviour is to "only update the branch pointer to match the merged branch" without creating a merge commit (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-merge). A join commit is only needed when the histories have actually diverged — when neither tip is an ancestor of the other — which is also why `--no-ff` exists: to force a merge commit in the fast-forwardable case for teams that want the branch visible as a bubble (https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Branching-Basic-Branching-and-Merging). The strongest distractor is the first one, because "merge always creates a commit" is the mental model most candidates carry, and it fails precisely here: there is nothing to join, so Git has nothing to commit. The new-hashes option describes rebase or cherry-pick, the only operations that rebuild commits, and the squash option describes `git merge --squash`, which is opt-in and leaves the changes staged instead of committing them.

mcqs.question: On `feature`, you run `git rebase main`. The rebase stops while replaying your third commit with `CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/checkout.ts`. You resolve with `git checkout --ours -- src/checkout.ts`. Which version of that file do you get?
options: The tree rebuilt so far — `main` plus the two commits already replayed — with this commit's change to the file dropped.
The file from `feature` before the rebase started, because `feature` was the branch you had checked out.
The file at the tip of `main`, unchanged, because during a rebase the upstream branch is the `ours` side.
The `theirs` side, because a rebase swaps the two sides and `--ours` therefore maps to the working branch.
mcqs.explanation: The git-rebase manual states it directly: "when a merge conflict happens, the side reported as ours is the so-far rebased series, starting with <upstream>, and theirs is the working branch. In other words, the sides are swapped" (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-rebase). Mechanically, Git has already checked out `main` and re-applies one commit at a time, so the index stage labelled `ours` holds the rebuilt tree and stage 3 holds the commit being replayed — `git show :2:src/checkout.ts` and `git show :3:src/checkout.ts` print both sides before you choose. `--ours` copies the whole stage-2 file, not just the conflicting hunks, so any other hunk this commit contributed to that file goes too. The strongest distractor is the second one: it carries the merge intuition ("I had `feature` checked out, so `ours` is me") into a rebase, which resolves every conflict to the wrong side and keeps `main`'s content while the commit messages survive, so nothing looks broken afterwards. The third option is the memorized simplification — at file granularity the rebuilt tree already contains your earlier replayed commits, so it is not `main`'s file — and the fourth confuses "the sides are swapped" with "the flags are remapped": the flags are not, which is why `--theirs` is the one that keeps the replayed commit's version, still worth reviewing by hand because it is whole-file too.

mcqs.question: `main` is shared, and a bad commit sits three commits behind the tip and was already pushed. A teammate proposes `git reset --hard <bad-commit>~1 && git push --force-with-lease`. Why is `git revert <bad-commit>` the right choice here?
options: Because `git reset` only accepts `HEAD~1`; to reach anything older you have to use `revert`.

Because `revert` adds an inverse commit so the tip only moves forward, which every existing clone can fast-forward, while `reset --hard` moves the ref backward and forces every clone and every branch cut from `main` to reconcile; `--force-with-lease` protects your own push from unseen remote changes, not the people who already pulled.
Because `reset --hard` deletes the bad commit's objects immediately and the change becomes unrecoverable, whereas `revert` keeps them; that is the only functional difference between the two.
Because `git restore --source=<bad-commit>^ -- .` rewrites the branch pointer and the index together, which is the same effect as `revert` with fewer commits.
mcqs.explanation: `git revert` computes the inverse of the target commit's change and records it as a new commit, so history only grows: a plain `git fetch` gives every collaborator a fast-forward, and the offending change is still identifiable in the log for the postmortem. `git reset` moves the branch ref itself, so on a shared branch the divergence is pushed onto everyone else, and their next merge can resurrect the reverted change. `--force-with-lease` only refuses to overwrite a push you have not seen; it says nothing about clones and branches that already contain the discarded commits. The strongest distractor is the object-deletion one, because it names a real command that looks destructive: reset does not delete objects, the reflog keeps them reachable, so a candidate who believes the risk is destruction picks the right command for the wrong reason and cannot explain when reset is actually fine — for a local commit nobody has pulled (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-reset, https://git-scm.com/docs/git-revert).

mcqs.question: A payment regression is reported in `src/payment.ts`. `git blame -L 80,95 -- src/payment.ts` attributes the suspicious line to last week's commit titled "chore: format with prettier". What is the correct reading of that output?
options: Blame is authoritative for origin, so the formatting commit introduced the regression; a bisect would only confirm it.

Blame reports the most recent commit that changed those lines, so a whitespace-only reformat can end up owning older logic; `git blame -w -C` traces the line back past whitespace and moved code, and only a bisect against a deterministic reproduction establishes which commit caused the regression.
Blame shows the commit that created the file, so the trail continues from the file's first revision and the formatting commit is irrelevant.
Blame attribution breaks on branches that contain merges, so the formatting commit is a false positive and only `git log -p --follow` on that single file can identify the regression.
mcqs.explanation: `git blame` answers "which revision last touched this line", not "which revision broke this behaviour" — a reformat, a line move, or a squash merge re-attributes lines whose logic is much older. `-w` ignores whitespace-only differences when matching a line to its parent and `-C` detects lines copied or moved in from another file, so together they push attribution back toward the real change (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-blame). Causation still needs a test: a bisect between a known-good and a known-bad revision, run against a deterministic reproduction, is what identifies the introducing commit. The strongest distractor is the first one, because blame output is precise and looks authoritative and a formatting commit genuinely does own the line in the default view; it confuses line attribution with causation, and the actual regression may live in a file blame never shows. The merge claim in the fourth option is also wrong: merges do not invalidate blame, they just require reading the attribution deliberately.

mcqs.question: You fix a bug on `main`, cherry-pick that commit onto a branch cut from the production tag `v2.8.3`, release it as `v2.8.4`, then forward-port the same patch back to `main`. What does Git know about the two copies of the fix?
options: Both copies exist as separate commits with different hashes, because cherry-pick re-applies the diff onto a new parent; `git merge` reasons about ancestry rather than patch identity, so it never deduplicates them, and `-x` plus `git cherry` exist precisely because Git does not track this.
Git records the source commit in the new commit's metadata, so a later merge between the lines detects the duplicate and drops it.
Cherry-pick preserves the original hash when the patch applies cleanly, so both branches share one commit object and the later merge is a no-op.
The second application overwrites the first, leaving a single commit with the newest author date, because both copies touch identical lines.
mcqs.explanation: Cherry-pick applies the change relative to the picked commit's parent and creates a new commit object on the current branch; the hash differs because the parent, tree, and timestamps differ, even though the diff is identical. Merge walks the commit graph and three-way-merges trees, so two identical diffs are just content that happens to agree — not shared ancestry. A side effect worth knowing: if both lines already carry the change, the merge is quiet about it, which is why the copies are easy to lose track of. `git cherry-pick -x` appends a "(cherry picked from commit ...)" trailer to the message and `git cherry` compares patch-ids, and both exist because deduplication is not automatic (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-cherry-pick, https://git-scm.com/docs/git-cherry). The strongest distractor is the metadata one, because `-x` really does record the source commit; but that is a message trailer, not graph metadata, so no merge consults it — and the hash-preservation option is impossible, since the hash covers the parent.

scenarios.prompt: A teammate ran this sequence on `feature/payment-flow` and now claims the rebase 'ate their feature'. Diagnose what actually happened to their changes, explain how to recover the pre-rebase state, and say how you would verify the recovered branch before anyone force-pushes.

code.code:
git checkout feature/payment-flow
git rebase main
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/checkout.ts
git checkout --ours -- src/checkout.ts   # teammate: "keep my version"
git add src/checkout.ts
git rebase --continue
# ...the same two commands for the three remaining conflicts...
git log --oneline -5
# 4 commits replayed, messages intact
git diff main -- src/checkout.ts
# (no output) the branch's version of the file now matches main

scenarios.modelAnswer:
**What happened.** `git rebase main` checked out `main` and re-applied the four feature commits on top of it, one at a time. At each conflict the manual's rule applies verbatim: "the side reported as ours is the so-far rebased series, starting with <upstream>, and theirs is the working branch. In other words, the sides are swapped" (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-rebase). The teammate's comment is therefore backwards — `--ours` kept main's `src/checkout.ts`, and `--theirs` is what would have kept their own version. Three details make this the worst class of failure: the rebase finished cleanly, so nothing reported an error; the four replayed commits still carry their messages, so `git log` looks correct; and `--ours` is a whole-file checkout of index stage 2, so every hunk of that file that only the feature had contributed disappeared with the conflicting one. The empty `git diff main -- src/checkout.ts` is the observable symptom: the file is byte-identical to main, which no payment-flow branch should be after four commits.

**Recovery.** The pre-rebase commits were never deleted; the branch ref, not the objects, moved. The authoritative anchor is the branch reflog: `git reflog show feature/payment-flow` ends with the `rebase (finish)` entry as `@{0}` and the original tip as `@{1}`, which is exactly the case the manual documents ("the previous branch tip ... is accessible using the reflog of the current branch"). `ORIG_HEAD` also points there because `git rebase` sets it when it starts, and in this transcript nothing else moved it — but the manual warns it is "not guaranteed to still point to that commit at the end of the rebase if other commands that change ORIG_HEAD (like git reset) are used during the rebase", so check it before trusting it:

```bash
git reflog show feature/payment-flow        # find the entry before 'rebase (finish)'
git log --oneline -4 feature/payment-flow@{1}   # should be the four original commits
git reset --hard feature/payment-flow@{1}       # or: git rev-parse ORIG_HEAD && git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD
```

`git rebase --abort` is not an option here, and that is worth stating explicitly: it resets HEAD to the original branch only while a rebase is in progress. Once the rebase has finished it fails with `fatal: no rebase in progress`, so after the fact the reflog/reflog-derived ref above is the only way back.

**Redo the rebase properly.** The mistake to avoid is choosing a side blind. At each conflict inspect before deciding: `git status` lists the conflicted paths, `git show :1:src/checkout.ts` is the version the patch was computed against, `:2:` is the rebuilt side and `:3:` the commit being replayed, and `git checkout --conflict=diff3 -- src/checkout.ts` (or `merge.conflictStyle=zdiff3`) puts the ancestor inside the markers so the intended combination is visible instead of guessed. Edit the file to the combined result, run the focused tests, `git add` it, `git rebase --continue`. Reach for `git rebase --skip` only when the commit's change is genuinely already in the base — skipping because a conflict is annoying deletes the change.

**Verify before pushing.** Prove the series came back rather than eyeballing `git log`: `git diff feature/payment-flow@{1} -- src/checkout.ts` must now be non-empty, the payment tests must pass, and `git range-diff <pre-rebase-tip>...HEAD` compares each original commit with its replayed counterpart — a damaged replay shows up as a `!` line with the exact hunk that changed, which is the audit the teammate skipped (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-range-diff). Only then `git push --force-with-lease`, and only after confirming nobody built on the rewritten commits; if someone did, they re-sync onto the new tip, and that coordination cost is the reason to do this while the branch is still personal.
rubric: Names the inversion: during a rebase `ours` is the so-far rebased series starting at `main` and `theirs` is the commit being replayed, the opposite of a merge.
Explains why the damage is silent and file-wide: the commits and their messages survive, and `--ours` copies the whole stage-2 file, so only the content is missing.
Recovers the pre-rebase tip from the branch reflog entry before `rebase (finish)` (or `ORIG_HEAD`), and notes `ORIG_HEAD` is only trustworthy if no other ORIG_HEAD-moving command ran.
Scopes `git rebase --abort` correctly: it restores the pre-rebase state only while the rebase is stopped, not after it completed.
Verifies with `git diff`/`git range-diff` plus tests before `git push --force-with-lease`, and coordinates with anyone who pulled the rewritten commits.

scenarios.prompt: Production on tag `v2.8.3` started throwing a payment-timeout regression, while `main` already carries about 40 unreleased commits. An on-call engineer ran the transcript below and is about to publish `v2.8.4`. List every defect in the sequence, then write the commands you would actually run to find the introducing commit against the deployed code and ship a hotfix that contains only the fix.

code.code:
# 1) find the regression
git switch main
git bisect start
git bisect good v2.8.2
git bisect run npm test -- --grep "payment timeout"

# 2) ship the hotfix
git switch -c hotfix/payment-timeout
git cherry-pick 9f3c1ab
git tag v2.8.4
git push origin hotfix/payment-timeout v2.8.4

scenarios.modelAnswer:
Four things are wrong before the first commit is even tested.

**The search is anchored to the wrong revision.** The engineer bisects from the tip of `main`, so the range runs from `v2.8.2` all the way through 40 commits that were never deployed. A failing-but-harmless unreleased commit lands inside the range and gets reported as the culprit, while the code that is actually in production is never isolated. The endpoints have to be the two tags, bad first: `git bisect start v2.8.3 v2.8.2` (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-bisect). Nothing here proves `v2.8.3` is bad either — reproduce the failure on the tag before starting the search.

**The check is not a bisect-safe test.** `npm test -- --grep "payment timeout"` runs a suite whose failure is a timeout, which usually means a live sandbox, real latency, or shared state: the same commit can flip between good and bad, and each flip poisons the search. Commits that fail to build also exit non-zero and get recorded as bad. The reproduction must be deterministic, offline, fast, and honest about the exit-code contract: 0 is good, 1–127 (except 125) is bad, 125 means "cannot test this revision", and any other status aborts the bisect — that is how a broken build is skipped instead of accused (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-bisect). The working tree must be clean first, or local edits travel across checkouts and contaminate results.

**There is no `git bisect reset`.** After `git bisect run`, HEAD is detached at the first bad commit. The very next line, `git switch -c hotfix/payment-timeout`, therefore branches the hotfix from a random mid-history commit — not from `v2.8.3`, and not even from `main`'s tip. That is the defect that would actually ship the wrong tree, and it is invisible until someone diffs the release against the tag.

**The hotfix has no provenance and no forward port.** `git cherry-pick 9f3c1ab` without `-x` leaves no trace of the source commit, the tag is created before anything verifies the built artifact, and the fix is never brought back to `main`, so the next release reintroduces the bug that production just paid for. Cherry-pick also applies the diff relative to its parent, so if `9f3c1ab` depends on unreleased refactors the patch can apply cleanly and still fail to compile or behave; the release diff needs review, not assumption.

What I would run:

```bash
git status                      # must be clean
git fetch --tags origin
git switch --detach v2.8.3      # reproduce on the deployed code first
./scripts/check-payment-timeout.sh   # deterministic, offline; exits 125 if untestable

git bisect start v2.8.3 v2.8.2
git bisect run ./scripts/check-payment-timeout.sh
git show <first-bad-commit>     # read the diff and confirm the causal link
git bisect reset                # leave the detached state behind

git switch -c hotfix/payment-timeout v2.8.3
git cherry-pick -x <fix-commit> # or hand-apply the minimal fix if the source commit depends on unreleased work
git diff v2.8.3..HEAD           # must contain only the fix
# run the release checks against the built artifact
git tag -a v2.8.4 -m "v2.8.4: payment timeout fix (<incident link>)"
git push origin hotfix/payment-timeout v2.8.4

git switch main
git cherry-pick -x <fix-commit> # forward-port; resolve drift deliberately
git push origin main
```

If the tag was already pushed wrong, the fix is a new tag plus a revert, not a rewritten one: a published tag that other systems may already resolve should not be moved.
rubric: Anchors the search to the deployed tags — bad `v2.8.3`, good `v2.8.2` — instead of `main`'s tip, and reproduces the failure on the released code before starting.
Makes the check deterministic and offline, respects the `git bisect run` exit-code contract including 125 for untestable revisions, and calls `git bisect reset` before branching.
Reads the candidate commit's diff and confirms the causal link with the focused test instead of trusting the bisect verdict alone.
Cuts the hotfix from the exact production tag and keeps its diff identical to the fix (cherry-pick `-x`, or a deliberate minimal re-apply) before tagging the artifact it verified.
Forward-ports the same fix to `main` and keeps provenance: annotated tag, recorded source commit, incident reference, coordinated push.
